draft.title: Building the periodic table
card: In the 1860s, Dmitri Mendeleev, a Russian chemist, listed the elements known at the time. He placed elements with similar properties together in the same row or column of a table.
Sometimes an element did not fit the pattern. Mendeleev left a gap instead of forcing it into the wrong place.
He used the pattern to predict that the gaps were elements not yet found. He also predicted what their properties would be like.
Later, scientists discovered new elements that matched his predictions. Each one filled a gap, which showed the pattern was useful.
draft.remember: Mendeleev's table sorted elements by their properties, and its gaps led to predictions that later discoveries filled.

a.q: Why did Mendeleev leave gaps in his table?
opts: He expected elements not yet found to fit there
He had run out of room for the known elements
The elements for those places had been used up
He did not know the properties of any elements
a.why: The gaps held places for elements he thought existed but had not been found. Running out of room is wrong, because the gaps came from breaks in the pattern of properties.
a.clue: Think about what a gap in a pattern might point to.

b.q: A new element is found that has the properties Mendeleev predicted for one gap. What does this show?
opts: His pattern could predict elements not yet found
His table was wrong and needed to be thrown out
Elements can only be sorted by their size
All the gaps in the table were now filled
b.why: A match between a find and a prediction shows the pattern worked. The table was not wrong. One new element fills one gap only, so it does not show all gaps were filled.
b.clue: A prediction that comes true supports the idea behind it.

a.best: He expected elements not yet found to fit there

b.best: His pattern could predict elements not yet found

problems.detail: 'Sometimes an element did not fit the pattern. Mendeleev left a gap instead of forcing it into the wrong place' reads as if the misfit element itself was left out or given a gap. In fact, when the next known element did not match the properties of a place, Mendeleev moved it on to a place it did fit and left that place empty for an undiscovered element. Rewording, for example 'when no known element fitted a place, he left it empty', would avoid this confusion.

check.summary: Both questions and explanations are sound. One card line is ambiguous: it could suggest the gap was for a known element that did not fit, rather than an empty place for an undiscovered element.

proposal.title: Building the periodic table
card: In 1869, Dmitri Mendeleev, a Russian chemist, made a table of the elements known at the time. He listed them roughly in order of the mass of their atoms and placed elements with similar properties together.
Sometimes no known element had the right properties for the next place in his table. He left that place empty and moved the element on to a place where its properties fitted.
He said each empty place was for an element not yet found. Using the elements around each gap, he also predicted what its properties would be.
Later, scientists discovered elements that matched his predictions and filled the gaps. For example, gallium, found in 1875, matched the element he predicted below aluminium.
proposal.remember: Gaps in a pattern can point to things not yet found, and Mendeleev's gaps were filled by later discoveries.

a.q: Why did Mendeleev leave some places in his table empty?
opts: He expected elements not yet found to fit there
He had run out of room for the known elements
He was unsure which way to order the elements
He left out elements that were too reactive
a.why: When no known element had the right properties for a place, he left it empty for an element still to be found. Running out of room is wrong, because the gaps came from the pattern of properties, not the size of the table.
a.clue: Think about what a gap in a pattern might point to.

b.q: A newly discovered element has the properties Mendeleev predicted for one gap. What does this show?
opts: His pattern could predict elements not yet found
His table was wrong and needed to be thrown out
Elements with similar properties do not sit together
Every gap in his table had now been filled
b.why: A discovery that matches a prediction shows the pattern worked. It does not show the table was wrong. One new element fills one gap only, so it does not show every gap was filled.
b.clue: A prediction that comes true supports the idea behind it.

a.best: He expected elements not yet found to fit there
